John Coltrane was an American jazz saxophonist, bandleader, and composer whose harmonic innovations, spiritual searching, and technical mastery made him one of the most revered and influential jazz musicians of all time.

He pioneered a revolutionary technique called sheets of sound, playing multiple notes simultaneously through rapid fingering, creating a cascade of harmonic color previously unheard in jazz. Coltrane pioneered modal jazz improvisation, abandoning traditional chord changes in favor of improvising over sustained scales. He was featured on "Kind of Blue" and developed this approach further in his own albums.

In 1964, he released "A Love Supreme," a masterpiece featuring four movements that declared jazz's spiritual and artistic legitimacy. It became one of jazz's best-selling and most revered albums. He composed "Giant Steps," whose rapid, complex harmonic progressions became a proving ground for saxophonists for generations and remains one of jazz's most challenging standards.

Coltrane played with Miles Davis from 1955 to 1960, then led his own quartet from 1960 to 1967, exploring increasingly experimental territory before his death at age forty. He was a spiritual seeker whose later work reflected his interest in Eastern philosophy, African music, and metaphysical themes. He studied under Thelonious Monk and absorbed his compositional and harmonic innovations, building upon and transcending Charlie Parker's harmonic language.
